headline: Bangladesh women face India in Asian Games semi-final today, seeking revenge after recent Asia Cup loss
summary: Bangladesh women's cricket team will battle strong favorites India in the Asian Games semi-final today, just ten days after a defeat in the Asia Cup.
details: Bangladesh women's cricket team is set to face India in the Asian Games semi-final today, a rematch just ten days after their defeat in the Asia Cup. The previous loss significantly impacted the team, even leading to captain Nigar Sultana stepping down from T20 captaincy.
The crucial match will kick off at 11 AM Bangladesh time in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. India, fresh off an Asia Cup victory, is widely considered the favorite for this encounter.
India's gold medal-winning T20 team last lost to Australia in June, maintaining a six-match winning streak since then. They comfortably defeated Japan by 8 wickets in the Asian Games quarter-finals.
Bangladesh, however, advanced to the semi-finals without playing their quarter-final match against China, which was abandoned due to rain. Their higher ranking secured their spot in the next round.

Historically, Bangladesh has won only three out of 25 T20 matches against India, including losses in this year's T20 World Cup and Asia Cup. For this match, Bangladesh will rely heavily on their bowlers to challenge the strong Indian side.

In two of their three victories against India, Bangladesh successfully restricted their opponents to under 120 runs. Spinners are expected to lead this effort, supported by pacer Marufa Akter, who is in excellent form, consistently taking wickets in her last six T20s with her new-ball swing.

headline_marked: [[US gains permanent control over Greenland's security]] in binding deal, bars Russia and China
headline: US gains permanent control over Greenland's security in binding deal, bars Russia and China
summary: The agreement, hailed by both the US and Denmark, aims to strengthen Arctic security by preventing rival nations from establishing military bases or making sensitive investments in the autonomous Danish territory.
details: The United States has secured a "binding" deal with Denmark, granting Washington "permanent control" over Greenland's security. This agreement explicitly bars Russia and China from establishing military bases or making sensitive investments in the Arctic territory.

US President Donald Trump has consistently advocated for Washington's control over Greenland for strategic reasons since January 2025, a stance that previously caused alarm for NATO ally Denmark and sparked significant pushback.
Both Denmark and Greenland, an autonomous Danish territory, have welcomed the deal. They are set to formally sign the agreement next week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen expressed optimism, stating the deal would replace a "long period of uncertainty" with a "binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and North Atlantic." He affirmed that the deal respects Denmark's "red lines" and is crucial given the evolving security landscape.

While Denmark maintains its sovereignty remains intact, Trump hailed the agreement as an "Infinite Life" deal, announcing immediate plans for a large US military buildup in the territory. He declared that no US adversary would ever have a base or military presence in Greenland without express US approval.

However, Danish commentators suggest Trump hasn't gained significantly new powers, noting that a 1951 defense pact (updated in 2004) already allowed the US to increase its military presence with prior notification to Denmark and Greenland.

The US State Department underscored the agreement's role in preventing China and Russia from establishing a foothold in Greenland, reflecting ongoing strategic competition in the warming Arctic region.

The deal follows a period of heightened tension when Trump had not ruled out using force to acquire the territory, causing anxiety within the EU and NATO. Subsequently, NATO launched a new mission to bolster Arctic security, seemingly to assuage US concerns.
